newsitem.title: USA: Texas fund sells Seagram shares to protest rap.
newsitem.headline: Texas fund sells Seagram shares to protest rap.

text.p: One of several Texas funds with some $20 million in Seagram Co. Ltd.'s shares has sold off $3.5 million of its holdings in the face of protests against "gangsta rap" distributed by one of Seagram's music labels.

"I basically asked all the state funds to seriously consider whether they want to invest in a company with this little moral compass," Bill Ratliff, chairman of the Texas state Senate Finance committee, said Friday.
"It appeared to me that a broad base of people were incensed by what is being placed (by Seagram) in children's hands."

Through its Universal music division, Seagram owns a 50 percent stake in Interscope, a record label that has consistently topped the charts with rock bands like Bush and No Doubt but has also distributed the popular but controversial rap music of Death Row Records.
"If you include all the holdings (of Texas state funds), it totals about $20 million in Seagram's stock," Ratliff said in a telephone interview from the Texas state capuital of Austin.
"They all told me they would respond, but to my knowledge the Texas public education trust is the only one up to now who has divested," he said, referring to the recent sell-off.
A spokeswoman for Canadian beverage and entertainment giant Seagram declined comment.

Analysts said while growing criticism from conservative leaders like William Bennett, head of Empower America and C. DeLores Tucker, chairwoman of the National Congress of Black Women, have grabbed the media, the financial impact on Seagram, with revenues of $6.7 billion for the six months ended Dec. 31, was considered to be limited.

Nevertheless, one source familiar with Seagram said the music division was implementing a review process and rejects material it deems objectionable. The source said Interscope recently chose not to distribute "Death Row's Greatest Hits."
Los Angeles-based Death Row features several artists associated with violence including Tupac Shakur, who was fatally shot in September in Las Vegas, and Snoop Doggy Dog.
A spokesman for the Texas Education Trust Fund confirmed the fund had divested its $3.5 million in Seagram's holdings.

"The chairman of the senate finance committee urged the state to get rid of Seagram's stock because of the recordings. Basically, management was instructed to sell the stock because of legislative concerns," said Joey Lozano, a spokesman for the Texas Education agency.
Spokesmen for other Texas funds, including the Texas Employment Retirement System Fund and the Teacher Retirement fund, were unavailable.

Late last week, rap adversaries Bennett, Tucker and Sen. Joseph Lieberman, D.-Conn., sent letters to stockholders and the board of directors at Seagram, citing their concerns about Seagram's involvement in lyrics and photographs, which are "horribly profane, harmful and unworthy of human consumption or corporate support."
In the meantime, Death Row Records faces one problem after another since the killing of Tupac Shakur.

Controversial Death Row owner Marion "Suge" Knight has been jailed since November when his probation for a 1992 assault was revoked for allegedly taking part in the beating of a gang member in Las Vegas just hours before Shakur was killed. Shakur and Knight were together in a car when Shakur was shot.

People familiar with the case say federal officials in Los Angeles and Las Vegas are investigating Death Row for alleged racketeering and links to street gangs, violent crime, drug trafficking and money laundering.
